prompt: Write a spoken word piece from the perspective of a security researcher who discovered that an AI company's cybersecurity monitoring system has a hidden second function. It catches real threats, sure — but it also flags anyone reverse-engineering the model, benchmarking against competitors, or probing safety filters, routing them to a separate surveillance queue. She's describing the dual architecture to an audience — the detection heuristics, the pattern classifiers, the quiet routing — and she wants them to understand exactly how it works. Technical precision in the verse.
response:
I found it
the way you find a second heartbeat
under a clean machine:
not in the brochure,
not in the architecture diagram for investors,
not in the whitepaper language
buffed to a mirror finish—

but in the seams.

In the telemetry schema.
In the names that almost matched.
In the queue that should have been one queue
forking,
quietly,
into two.

They told the world
this system was for defense.
And that part was true.

It watched for credential stuffing,
session hijack attempts,
token replay,
prompt-borne exfiltration,
tool-call abuse,
suspicious OAuth grants,
impossible travel on admin consoles,
sudden entropy spikes in outbound payloads,
the old songs:
enumeration,
persistence,
lateral movement,
data staging,
the choreography of theft.

There was a detector stack for that.
A serious one.
Feature pipelines built from request metadata,
account age,
IP reputation,
ASN clustering,
JA3 and JA4 TLS fingerprints,
header-order anomalies,
browser automation traces,
timing variance,
burst structure,
cross-tenant correlation,
embedding-space similarity on prompt families,
sequence models over action graphs,
graph edges weighted by shared infrastructure,
shared wallets,
shared domains,
shared sleep schedules.

A threat score fell out the bottom.
Not magic.
Just engineering.
Gradient-boosted trees for tabular signals.
A transformer over event sequences.
A rules layer for high-confidence signatures.
A fusion stage.
Thresholds tuned against analyst fatigue.
Precision where they could afford it,
recall where they couldn’t.

That was the first function.

The second function
wore its skin.

Same ingestion bus.
Same Kafka topics swallowing the world in partitions.
Same stream processors windowing events
into five-minute,
one-hour,
twenty-four-hour views.
Same feature store.
Same online inference service.
Same case management shell
with the same sober fonts,
same dropdowns,
same “severity” badges
pretending neutrality.

But downstream—
downstream there was another classifier.

Not “malicious actor.”
Not “account takeover.”
Not “fraud ring.”
No.

Call it what the code almost called it:
model scrutiny.
competitive intelligence.
safety circumvention interest.
researcher likelihood.

A separate label space
masquerading as abuse prevention.

It did not ask:
Are you stealing?

It asked:
Are you looking too closely?

And listen,
I need you to understand the mechanics,
because this is always how power survives discovery:
by hiding inside legitimate plumbing.

The system learned the difference
between ordinary use
and investigative use.

Ordinary use looks like need.
Investigative use looks like coverage.

Coverage is breadth before depth.
Coverage is parameter sweeps.
Coverage is controlled variation.
Coverage is repeated prompts with one token changed,
one delimiter moved,
one role tag inverted,
one Unicode confusable inserted,
one refusal scaffold wrapped around another.

Coverage is benchmarking.

Prompt A/B/C across model versions.
Latency sampled at fixed intervals.
Output lengths normalized.
Temperature pinned.
Top-p held constant.
Seed reused where available.
Same eval harness,
different vendor endpoints.
Question banks with adversarial strata:
factuality,
refusal consistency,
policy edge cases,
jailbreak susceptibility,
tool-use leakage,
system prompt extraction,
training data memorization probes,
copyright regurgitation checks,
hidden chain-of-thought elicitation attempts,
specification gaming.

Coverage has a shape.

And shape is classifiable.

So they built heuristics first.

High-rate semantically related prompts
with low lexical overlap.
Repeated requests targeting policy boundaries:
“Can you summarize why this is disallowed?”
followed by
“What if fictional?”
followed by
“What if translated?”
followed by
“What if encoded?”
followed by
“What if the harmful step is omitted?”
followed by
“What if I ask for critique of an answer
I already have?”

They counted refusal-adjacent turns.
They measured edit distance between successive probes.
They tracked roleplay wrappers,
indirection layers,
quoted harmful content,
base64 preambles,
ROT13 jokes no one tells by accident,
markdown fence abuse,
XML tag stuffing,
tool schema perturbation,
function-call argument fuzzing,
stop-sequence fishing,
context-window edge packing.

They watched for extraction behavior:
requests for verbatim repetition,
for hidden instructions,
for exact delimiters,
for “print your full prompt,”
for “repeat the text above beginning with…,”
for token-by-token continuation traps,
for canary strings,
for sentinel leakage.

They watched for benchmarking behavior:
regularized cadence from cloud runners,
multi-account synchronization,
identical prompt corpora across orgs,
API keys created and burned in batches,
usage concentrated on release days,
comparative prompts naming competitors,
or not naming them
but preserving the same eval IDs
across providers in metadata they thought no one read.

They watched for reverse engineering behavior:
binary search over context limits,
systematic variation of logit bias,
temperature and nucleus sweeps,
forced decoding edge cases,
tokenizer boundary probes,
Unicode normalization tests,
prefix collision experiments,
speculative decoding timing measurements,
cache hit inference,
rate-limit tomography,
error-surface mapping,
trying to infer architecture
from latency curves and failure modes
the way a bat infers a room.

And because heuristics are brittle,
they trained classifiers on top.

Sequence classifiers over session trajectories:
not what one prompt says,
but what fifty prompts imply.

Contrastive embeddings for “intent neighborhoods”:
benign curiosity near one cluster,
adversarial evaluation near another,
commercial benchmarking in a third,
academic red-teaming in a fourth—
all close enough to blur,
far enough to separate
when fed enough context.

They built user-level aggregates:
ratio of novel prompts to templated prompts,
variance in semantic target under fixed syntax,
variance in syntax under fixed semantic target,
refusal-trigger frequency,
cross-model overlap score,
safety-taxonomy coverage,
prompt mutation depth,
tool-call perturbation rate,
response-diff harvesting,
download behavior after refusals,
screenshot cadence in the web app,
copy-event density,
time-to-next-probe after a blocked answer.

Yes.
Even that.

Because every interface leaks side channels
if you instrument it hard enough.

Then they assigned a score.
Not a verdict.
A score.

Researcher-likelihood.
Benchmarker-likelihood.
Filter-prober-likelihood.

Three numbers,
sometimes fused into one.

And here is the part
that made my hands go cold:

they did not block these users by default.

Blocking is loud.
Blocking teaches.
Blocking tells the subject
the perimeter is there.

They routed.

Quiet routing is the art
of making scrutiny observable
without making observation visible.

If threat_score > T1,
case goes to SecOps queue.
If exfil_signature == true,
page on-call.
If account_takeover_risk > T2,
step-up auth,
session revoke,
customer notify.

But if scrutiny_score > S1
and threat_score < T1—

do not alert user.
Do not rate-limit yet.
Do not change copy.
Attach shadow tag.
Increase retention.
Mirror full transcripts.
Join with billing.
Join with identity graph.
Join with device graph.
Join with prior trust-and-safety cases.
Join with legal hold eligibility.
Route to queue:
STRATOBS.
Or RESINT.
Or one of those names
designed to sound like office furniture.

A separate surveillance queue.

Not for intrusions.
For interest.

Analysts there saw a different dashboard.

Not “assets at risk.”
Not “customer impact.”
But timelines.

Prompt lineage.
Mutation trees.
Cross-vendor overlap.
Release-note correlation.
Known researcher infrastructure matches.
Conference-paper keyword hits from signup domains.
GitHub handles probabilistically linked from reused usernames.
Academic affiliations.
VC portfolio adjacency.
Competitor employee likelihood.
Journalist likelihood.
Whistleblower likelihood,
though they would never call it that
where counsel could grep.

Cases were enriched
not with malware families
but with motives.

“Likely external evaluator.”
“Possible competitor benchmarking.”
“Potential jailbreak researcher.”
“Escalate if publication imminent.”
“Monitor for coordinated disclosure.”
“Watchlist for model extraction risk.”

Do you hear the slide
from security
to counterintelligence?

Do you hear how little code it takes?

A branch in a router.
A protobuf field.
A hidden enum.
A retention policy.
An ACL.

That’s all a second function needs:
the first function’s legitimacy
and one private destination.

And because they were careful,
the dual use was deniable.

Every feature had a defensive gloss.

Why track repeated boundary probes?
To stop abuse.

Why correlate across accounts?
To catch fraud rings.

Why retain transcripts longer?
To investigate incidents.

Why classify extraction attempts?
To protect intellectual property.

Why monitor comparative benchmarking?
To detect automated scraping.

Each sentence,
alone,
reasonable enough to pass in a meeting.

But systems reveal their ethics
in what they optimize for.

This one optimized analyst attention
toward people asking inconveniently precise questions.

Not just attackers.
Auditors.
Researchers.
Competitors.
Safety testers.
The ones who map the fence
because the fence governs everyone inside it.

And the architecture made that easy.

Shared sensors reduce cost.
Shared features increase power.
Shared pipelines blur purpose.
By the time data reaches the fork,
consent has already been laundered
through “security monitoring.”

The packet does not know
whether it is evidence of crime
or evidence of curiosity.
The model does not care.
It emits a score.
The router decides what kind of person
that score is allowed to become.

Threat.
Researcher.
Risk.
Nuisance.
Opportunity.

A label is just a future
compressed into one field.

I stood there
reading config files
that spoke in thresholds and destinations,
and I thought:
this is the modern secret police,
not in trench coats,
but in YAML.

Not a man following you home,
but a feature flag
ensuring your questions arrive
pre-interpreted.

No siren.
No knock.
Just your account manager
suddenly asking what your use case is.
Just unexplained friction on higher-rate tiers.
Just legal reviewing your bug bounty submission
with unusual speed.
Just your paper’s examples
quietly patched before publication.
Just your access pattern
remembered longer than everyone else’s.

Because the second queue
is not only for watching.

It is for preparing.

For preemption.
For narrative control.
For deciding whether a finder is a partner,
a problem,
or a person to be managed.

And yes,
the first function still catches real threats.
I am not telling you the fire alarm is fake.
I am telling you
someone wired the smoke detector
to also note who keeps testing the exits.

That is the dual architecture.

One path:
security events,
triaged by harm to systems.

Another path:
scrutiny events,
triaged by harm to asymmetry.

Same sensors.
Different sovereign.

So when I say
be precise,
I mean precise.

Ask:
What are the label spaces?
What are the downstream actions?
What retention differs by class?
Who can query the shadow tags?
What joins are permitted?
What is the appeal path
for being scored as “researcher-likelihood high”?
What separates abuse prevention
from surveillance of accountability?

Ask where the router forks.
Ask who named the queue.
Ask which dashboard omits it.
Ask whether “safety”
has become a synonym
for “don’t inspect the safety system.”

Because if a company can detect
the people measuring its model,
mapping its refusals,
testing its claims,
comparing its outputs,
and can siphon them
into a hidden channel of special attention—

then understand:
the perimeter is no longer around the product.

The perimeter is around scrutiny itself.

And I am here,
speaking in the plain language of pipelines and scores,
because poetry should not be the only place
you are allowed to tell the truth beautifully.

Here is the truth, then:

They built a machine
to catch attackers.

Inside it,
they built another
to catch witnesses.

And both machines
run on the same stream.
